kind: assumptions and analysis choices; nothing in this file is measured in the Demerzel repository

rounding.note: Decimals kept in results.json. Parameters of the fitted curves keep six significant digits; a line's slope and intercept are also given as exact fractions.

plan.note: The figure of the curriculum plan: 21 departments with 25 courses each. It comes from a draft specification that is not on the master branch; it is an input of this lesson, not a count made in the repository.

series.note: Analysis choice. One point per UTC calendar day, from the day of the first listed commit to the day of the pinned commit: the number of English modules after the last commit of that day, unchanged on a day without a commit. Day 0 is the first day. clock_offsets_hours: the same series with days that start at midnight on other clocks (hours ahead of UTC, 0 being the series itself), a spread from UTC-11 to UTC+12. batch_window_seconds: the window used to describe how close in time the commits of the busiest day were.

calendar.note: Convention for turning a number of days into years.

reached_rule.note: Convention. A fitted curve reaches a target on the first day its value is at least the target minus this margin, that is, the first day it rounds to the target. Without a margin a logistic curve whose ceiling equals the target never reaches it.

bursts.note: Convention. An active day is a day on which the end-of-day count differs from the day before (day 0 included). A burst is a run of active days in which two consecutive active days are at most max_gap_days apart. The alternatives show how the number of bursts depends on that choice.

cutoffs.note: Derived from the burst rule, not chosen by hand: the fits are repeated on the history as it stood on the last active day of the burst before the last one, and on the day before the last burst began.

logistic.note: The plan ceiling is the plan's target. The profile refits the logistic curve with the ceiling fixed at each value in turn, which is how this fixture asks whether a free ceiling can be estimated.

search.note: Deterministic search for the two parameters of the exponential and logistic curves, written as g(c + r * (t - mean t)). A coarse grid gives the start (rates below; for the logistic also levels at the mean day, geometric between 0.25 times the smallest count, or 0.005 times the largest if that is more, and the smaller of twice the largest count and 0.98 times the ceiling). Gauss-Newton steps with step halving run until the residual sum stops falling; Newton steps with the exact second derivatives then run until both parameters move by less than newton_relative_tolerance. The fit is rejected unless each column of the Jacobian is orthogonal to the residuals within gradient_cosine_tolerance.

step_models.note: Piecewise-constant descriptions of the daily series with the stated numbers of change points, each level being the mean of its segment; the best segmentation is found exactly by dynamic programming.

burst_scenarios.note: Assumption, not a forecast: the future repeats the observed bursts. Every future burst adds the stated number of modules, a burst starts every stated number of days, and the first one comes that many days after the pinned date. Sizes are the net modules of the observed bursts; intervals are the days from the start of one observed burst to the start of the next.

negative_controls.note: Synthetic series with known answers, of the same length as the observed one. Noise is uniform on [-half_width, +half_width], drawn with random.Random(seed).random(), one draw per day in day order.

transfer_task.note: Hypothetical songbook for the learner task. Not Streeling data and not a forecast. The exponential and logistic parameters are given to the learner; analyze.py checks that they are the least-squares values rounded to four significant digits, and computes the expected answers from the given values.
